claim: The DR whitepaper says asynchronous data replication in the multi-site active/active strategy enables near-zero RPO, and it names Aurora global database as an example service.
question: What RPO does asynchronous replication give in a multi-site active/active DR strategy, according to the DR whitepaper?

evidence.quote: Asynchronous data replication with this strategy enables near-zero RPO.

note: d27-059. The same paragraph says Aurora global database can replicate to up to five secondary Regions; the Aurora guide now says 10, so the whitepaper wording is older.

claim: The DR whitepaper says multi-site active/active is the most complex and costly DR approach, but it can reduce recovery time to near zero for most disasters; data corruption may still need backups, which usually means a non-zero recovery point.
question: What is the cost and recovery-time trade-off of multi-site active/active disaster recovery?

values.display: reduce your recovery time to near zero for most disasters

evidence.quote: This approach is the most complex and costly approach to disaster recovery, but it can reduce your recovery time to near zero for most disasters with the correct technology choices and implementation (however data corruption may need to rely on backups, which usually results in a non-zero recovery point).

claim: In the warm standby strategy a scaled down but fully functional copy of the production environment runs in another Region, which extends the pilot light idea and decreases the time to recovery because the workload is always on.
question: Why does warm standby recover faster than pilot light, according to the DR whitepaper?

evidence.quote: This approach extends the pilot light concept and decreases the time to recovery because your workload is always-on in another Region.

claim: In the pilot light strategy the core infrastructure is always available, and unlike backup and restore you can quickly provision a full scale production environment by switching on and scaling out the application servers.
question: What is always available in a pilot light disaster recovery strategy?

values.display: your core infrastructure is always available

qualifiers.condition: data stores such as databases are always on; application servers are switched off

evidence.quote: Unlike the backup and restore approach, your core infrastructure is always available and you always have the option to quickly provision a full scale production environment by switching on and scaling out your application servers.

claim: An Aurora DB cluster is fault tolerant by design: it can tolerate the failure of an Availability Zone without any loss of data and with only a brief interruption of service.
question: What happens to an Aurora DB cluster when a whole Availability Zone fails?

values.display: without any loss of data and only a brief interruption of service

qualifiers.scope: Aurora DB cluster within one Region

evidence.quote: This functionality means that your DB cluster can tolerate a failure of an Availability Zone without any loss of data and only a brief interruption of service.

note: d27-041. Compare RDS Multi-AZ: a standby in another Availability Zone.

claim: Aurora Global Database supports managed minor version upgrades: you start the upgrade in the console, SDK or CLI and all global clusters, across Regions, are upgraded to the selected minor version.
question: What does the February 2026 change let you do for the minor version upgrade of an Aurora global database?

qualifiers.condition: announced 2026-02-10; currently supported only for Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible engines

evidence.quote: You can now perform managed minor version upgrades through the AWS Management Console, SDK, or CLI and all the global clusters, across Regions, are upgraded to the selected minor version, eliminating the need to manually upgrade each cluster individually.

note: The same post says a global database spans up to 11 AWS Regions, which matches one primary plus 10 secondary Regions. Before this change each cluster was upgraded one by one.

claim: Managed minor version upgrades for Aurora Global Database are currently supported only for Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible engines.
question: Which Aurora engines support managed minor version upgrades for a global database?

values.display: only supported for Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible engines

evidence.quote: This capability is currently only supported for Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible engines and available in all commercial AWS Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

claim: Aurora MySQL delayed replication lets you configure a binlog replica to lag behind its source by a set period of time, as a safeguard against human error and logical data corruption.
question: What does Aurora MySQL delayed replication provide?

values.display: intentionally lag behind its source by a set period of time

evidence.quote: Delayed replication lets you configure a binlog replica to intentionally lag behind its source by a set period of time, giving you a simple safeguard against human error and logical data corruption.

claim: Multi-source replication and delayed replication are supported on Aurora MySQL version 8.4.8 and higher, in all AWS Regions where Aurora MySQL is available.
question: Which Aurora MySQL versions support multi-source and delayed replication?

evidence.quote: Multi-source replication and Delayed replication are supported on Aurora MySQL version 8.4.8 and higher, in all AWS Regions where Aurora MySQL is available.
